title: Do MIB Circuit Localization Methods Agree on the Same Prompts They Fail On?

original_idea.problem: Different circuit localization methods may fail on systematically different prompt types.
original_idea.direction: Run at least two MIB methods (attribution patching and ACDC) on the four MIB tasks. Record per-prompt performance. Compute failure correlation. Cluster failing prompts by linguistic features.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if methods fail on different prompts, ensembling could improve coverage. If they fail on the same prompts, those represent hard frontiers. The safety relevance is through improving circuit discovery reliability, which is a step removed from direct safety applications.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Running ACDC and attribution patching requires familiarity with circuit discovery tools. The MIB benchmark code exists but integrating it, extracting per-prompt results, and performing failure correlation analysis requires intermediate-to-advanced interpretability experience.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Two methods on four tasks is well-defined, but setting up both methods and extracting per-prompt results from their evaluation code may require significant engineering effort. The clustering analysis adds another workstream.

novelty.reasoning: The MIB benchmark (arXiv:2504.13151, ICML 2025) and the BlackboxNLP 2025 shared task directly compare circuit localization methods (attribution patching, ACDC, EAP-IG, mask optimization, etc.) on four tasks and five models. The shared task findings (arXiv:2511.18409) show that methods differ in effectiveness per task/model (e.g., EActP dominates for IOI on GPT-2 but not Qwen). Ensemble strategies (arXiv:2510.06811) were explored. However, the specific per-prompt failure correlation analysis — do methods fail on the same individual prompts? — and clustering of failing prompts by linguistic features has not been published. The benchmark provides aggregate comparisons, not per-prompt failure analysis.

evidence: Mueller et al. (2025). MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark. arXiv:2504.13151.
